---
title: "Stable Sharding Versus Hot Keys"
description: "Advanced system-design reasoning with formal constraints and a small tested code example."
---

## Interview challenge

A distributed key-value store has three nodes. Adding a fourth should not move almost every key. But if a famous user's profile consumes 80% of traffic, moving keys evenly by count will **not** balance CPU.

The surprising point: **stable assignment and balanced load are different optimisation objectives**.

## Start with rendezvous hashing

For key $k$ and node $n$, compute a deterministic score $h(k,n)$. Assign the key to the node with the highest score:

$$
n^*(k)=\arg\max_{n\in N}h(k,n).
$$

When one node disappears, keys previously assigned to **other nodes** retain their winner: all surviving scores are unchanged. Only keys whose winner was removed need reassignment.

## Actual small implementation

~~~ts
const nodes = ['A','B','C'];
const before = rendezvous('user:7',nodes);
const after = rendezvous('user:7',['A','B']);
// If before was A or B, it must stay the same after removal.
~~~

GET /lab/shard?key=user:7 demonstrates selection. The test checks this minimal-movement property over hundreds of keys. The lab uses simple FNV-like hashing for reproducibility, **not a cryptographic hash**.

## Now change just one assumption

Suppose ten thousand keys are evenly assigned, but the key for one high-profile account receives 80% of requests. A mathematically uniform key distribution can still leave a single node overloaded.

$$
\operatorname{load}(n)=\sum_{k:\,n^*(k)=n}r_k\,c_k
$$

where $r_k$ is request rate and $c_k$ per-request compute cost. Even if the number of keys per node is equal, this sum can be wildly unequal.

## The difficult but simple answer

Separate **key ownership** from **read-serving capacity**. For a read-heavy hot key, replicate its cached value to multiple serving nodes, distribute reads to replicas, and keep a clear authoritative write path and invalidation/version policy. For write-hot data, naive replication does not solve contention on one ordered key; consider partitioning the business entity or changing the aggregation model.

Google Research studied **consistent hashing with bounded loads**, which explicitly addresses the risk that an unbounded hash allocation overloads some servers. That is a more precise target than assuming consistent hashing 'balances traffic'.

## Interview follow-ups

- How does a new node affect routing? Only keys that select it as the new maximum should move in rendezvous hashing.
- What if the key changes value every millisecond? Read replicas may become stale; freshness and fanout are the new bottleneck.
- Why not replicate every key ten times? Memory cost, write propagation and cache-consistency complexity increase.

## Mathematical Abstraction

$$
\min\ \operatorname{KeysMoved}(N\to N')
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\max_{n\in N'}\operatorname{load}(n)\leq C_n.
$$

This expresses two competing goals: minimise movement after topology changes and respect per-node capacity. Plain rendezvous hashing addresses the first; it does not enforce the capacity constraint.

**Research:** Google Research, [Consistent Hashing with Bounded Loads](https://research.google/blog/consistent-hashing-with-bounded-loads/).
